I woke up to the sound of the refrigerator humming, which is the most honest sound in any house. It does not care if you are late, if you are sad, if you had a dream you can’t remember. It just hums. I lay there for a minute longer than I intended, watching the light from the streetlamp move across the ceiling as a car passed outside. The light made a thin, amber line that crawled across the plaster and then vanished. It felt like a small, private weather.

I have been thinking a lot lately about how much of life is made up of these tiny, unrecorded events. The way the kettle clicks off. The way a certain kind of paper feels when you run your thumb across it. The way people say “I’m fine” with a slight lift at the end of the word, as if the fine-ness is a question. We are trained to look for the big moments, the narrative peaks, the before-and-after. We collect them like souvenirs. But the actual texture of being alive is granular, and it happens in the gaps between the things we are supposed to remember.

This morning I made coffee and burned the first batch. Not because I was careless, but because I was thinking about a conversation I had with my mother three years ago about whether she ever regrets moving to the coast. She said no, but she said it in a way that meant yes, a little. I stood at the stove with the grounds blooming in the filter and I could smell the char and I could hear the faint traffic from the street below and I thought, this is what memory does. It intrudes without permission and makes the present slightly foreign.

There is a particular kind of tiredness that comes from living in a world that wants you to be productive all the time. It is not the tiredness of physical labor, though that is real and worthy. It is a tiredness of attention. Your attention is asked for constantly, by notifications, by headlines, by people who need an immediate response. And so you learn to ration it, to put it where it will get the most return. But attention, like any muscle, atrophies when it is only used for extraction. It needs idle time. It needs to be allowed to wander.

I tried walking without a destination yesterday. I left the house with no phone, no podcast, no route planned. Just the vague intention to be back by lunch. The first ten minutes were awkward. My body kept trying to fill the silence with a list of tasks. Do the dishes. Reply to that email. Buy more toothpaste. I let the list run its course and then let it fade. After about twenty minutes, something shifted. I started noticing the architecture of the ordinary. The way the mailboxes on my block are all slightly different colors, as if each house decided on its own what kind of optimism it could afford. The way the ivy grows in a particular seam on the brick building across the street, finding a crack that no one intended to be a doorway.

I stopped at a corner store I never go into because it is a little farther than the one I usually use. The bell over the door jingled. The air inside was cool and smelled faintly of cardboard and citrus. A man was stocking oranges, turning each one gently as if checking for bruises. He saw me looking and nodded. I nodded back. That was the whole interaction. It contained, I think, a great deal more honesty than most of my longer conversations. We were both just present in the same small, conditioned space, acknowledging each other without demanding anything.

I bought a banana and a pack of gum I didn’t need. I stood at the counter for a moment too long, not because I was indecisive, but because I liked the pause. The cashier was a teenager with a chipped nail polish and a name tag that said “Milo.” He scanned my items, said thank you, and I said thank you back. On the street again, the banana felt heavy in my hand. The skin was yellow with a few green spots. I thought about the tree it came from, and the truck that brought it, and the hands that touched it before mine. That chain of touch is invisible until you decide to look for it.

People often ask me what I write about. I tell them I write about things. That answer is true and useless. I write about the way light falls on a kitchen table at 4 p.m. in February. I write about the small negotiations we make with ourselves to get out of bed. I write about the moment when you realize you have been holding your breath while reading something difficult. I write about how grief is not a storm but a change in air pressure, you only notice it when you try to open a window.

There is a comfort in specificity. The world is too large to hold in its totality, so we hold it in fragments. The smell of rain on hot asphalt. The sound of a key turning in a lock. The particular blue of a chipped mug that you keep because it fits your hand. These fragments accumulate into a kind of private map. If you lose the map, you can still navigate by the landmarks you have memorized in your body.

I think about the people who live in the buildings I pass every day. The woman on the third floor who waters her plants at exactly 7:30 every evening, even in winter. The man who plays the same piano piece through his window on Sundays, badly but with enthusiasm. I will never know their names. I will never know if they are happy. But they are part of the texture of my life, and I am part of theirs, in the way that all anonymous neighbors are part of each other’s stories. We are the background characters in each other’s novels, and sometimes, if we are lucky, we get a line of dialogue.

There is a temptation to believe that meaning is always found in the extraordinary. That you have to travel, or fall in love, or suffer, or create something large to have a life worth noting. I am not sure I believe that anymore. I think meaning is also found in repetition. In making the bed. In watering the plant. In checking the mailbox even though you know the bill is inside. The repetition is not empty. It is a kind of prayer, a way of saying: I am here, this matters, I will tend to it.

I have a friend who keeps a notebook where she writes down one true sentence a day. Not a profound sentence, just a true one. “The cat slept on my laundry.” “I cried in the grocery store because the onions were too cheap.” “I felt brave for five minutes.” She says it helps her remember that she existed on days when nothing big happened. I have started doing something similar, though mine is messier. Sometimes I write it on receipts. Sometimes I say it out loud to the ceiling. The point is not to create a record. The point is to practice attention.

The afternoon light is changing now. The amber line on the ceiling is gone. The refrigerator is still humming. I have a list of things I should do, and I will probably do some of them, and I will probably forget some of them. That is fine. The world does not require me to be efficient. It requires me to be present enough to notice when the banana is ripe, when the ivy finds a crack, when a stranger nods at me in a corner store.

If you ask me what I want for the rest of my life, I want more of these small, unremarkable moments. I want to be less afraid of boredom. I want to let my mind wander without immediately catching it and putting it to work. I want to learn the names of the trees on my block. I want to remember the faces of the cashiers. I want to be the kind of person who can sit on a bench and watch people walk by without needing to explain why.

There is a Japanese word, komorebi, for the way sunlight filters through leaves. It is a word for a thing that is not permanent, not controllable, not useful in any practical sense. It just is. I think we need more words like that. More words for the fleeting, the quiet, the in-between. More permission to stand still and watch light move across a ceiling.

I am going to drink the coffee I just made, the second batch, which is fine. The mug is chipped on the rim, and it fits my hand. The steam rises and disappears. The day is still young, and it is already full of things I will never write down, and that is okay. The world is large enough to hold both the stories we tell and the ones we don’t.

I think that is enough for now. The refrigerator hums. The light moves. I am here.
